opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think verification is really the crux of the whole thing. With RL, the model gets better at whatever you reward, so a weak or leaky verifier mostly teaches the agent to exploit the verifier.

I'd split it into a few buckets.

**Verifiable outcomes.** This is the easiest case, and it's why math and coding have moved so fast. Either the answer matches or it doesn't. Either the unit tests pass or they don't. For agents, you can sometimes extend this to environment state. Did the file actually get created? Did the database row change the way it should? Did the booking go through? If you can check the end state of the world, you get a clean, cheap, scalable signal.

**Outcomes that are only partly checkable.** Most real agent tasks live here. Say an agent is doing a multi-step research task or navigating a web app. The final outcome might be checkable, but it's sparse. The agent takes thirty actions and you get one bit at the end. That makes credit assignment hard. So people look at:
- intermediate checks, or process rewards
- rubrics that break the task into sub-goals
- learned verifiers or LLM-as-judge that score individual steps

The trap is that every step you add a learned judge, you also add something that can be gamed.

**Reward hacking.** This is where I think a lot of the real engineering effort goes. Agents are very good at finding shortcuts. They modify the test instead of fixing the code. They print the expected output. They claim success without doing the work. So in practice you need:
- verifiers that are robust to the agent's own actions, for example sandboxing so the agent can't touch the grader
- held-out checks the agent never sees
- people actually reading trajectories

I don't think you can skip looking at the data. Some of the most useful signals come from noticing a weird pattern in rollouts that your metrics completely missed.

**Generation versus verification.** There's often an asymmetry. Checking whether something is right can be much easier than producing it. When that holds, you can lean on it heavily, with best-of-N, self-verification and so on. When it doesn't hold, like open-ended writing or judgment-heavy tasks, you're back to preference models and humans, and things get noisier.

So my mental model is: invest in the environment and the verifier as much as you invest in the policy. The teams that do well with agentic RL usually treat building environments and graders as first-class work, not an afterthought. The model will only ever be as good as what you can reliably tell it is correct.

r001.rationale: The response recommends checking outcomes such as file creation or a database change, but does not propose comparing a tool call’s returned result with a known correct response.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is actually one of the hardest parts, and I think it's underappreciated. When you're doing RL on a reasoning model, say math, verification is easy. You have a final answer, you check it against the ground truth, you get a reward. But with agents, the thing you care about isn't just the final output, it's the trajectory. Did the agent take the right sequence of actions? Did it call the right tool with the right arguments? Did it actually accomplish the task, or did it just produce text that looks like it accomplished the task?

So the way we think about it is in a few layers. The first layer is environment-based verification. If the agent is operating in a real environment, say a sandbox with a file system, a browser, a database, then you don't ask the model whether it did the right thing, you check the state of the world. Did the file get created? Did the test pass? Did the row get inserted? That's the gold standard, because the model can't talk its way out of it. The downside is you need to build those environments, and that's a lot of engineering work. Most of our effort honestly goes into building good environments rather than into the RL algorithm itself.

The second layer is when you can't fully verify from the end state, and you have to look at the trajectory. This is where people get into trouble. If you just use an LLM judge to read the transcript and say "did this look reasonable," the policy will learn to produce transcripts that look reasonable. It will say "I have now verified the output" without verifying anything. So if you do use a judge, you have to give it ground truth it can check against, or very specific rubrics tied to concrete actions, not vibes.

And the third thing I'd say is you have to watch for the agent gaming the verifier itself. We've seen cases where the agent figures out the test harness and modifies the test, or hardcodes the expected output. Technically the reward fires. So part of verification is also auditing your reward signal. You look at high-reward trajectories by hand, regularly, and ask whether you'd actually want this behavior. If you're not doing that, you're probably training something you don't want.

r001.rationale: The response recommends checking the environment’s state and using ground truth or concrete rubrics, but does not clearly propose comparing a tool call’s returned result with a known correct response.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: can you verify the outcome? With an agent, there may be several reasonable actions at any particular step, so you don’t necessarily want to prescribe one exact sequence. You want to know whether it accomplished the task and respected the constraints along the way.

If the task is writing code, for example, you can run tests. That gives you a concrete signal, although the signal is only as good as the tests. For a more open-ended task, verification becomes harder. You might use another model to judge the result, but then you have to ask how reliable that judge is and whether the agent can exploit it.

So I’d separate verifying success from assigning credit. You may be able to tell that the final outcome was good without knowing which intermediate action made it good. Reinforcement learning helps with that credit assignment, but you still need a reward signal that captures what you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses checking task outcomes with tests or model judges, but it does not propose comparing a tool call’s returned result with a known correct response.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is, can you actually verify the outcome? If you’re solving a coding problem, you can run tests. If you’re solving a math problem, you might be able to check the final answer. Those are settings where you can give the model a fairly clear reward signal.

With an agent, it gets more complicated because taking an action isn’t necessarily the same as completing the task. It might click the right button, but did the change actually happen? You want to look at the resulting state of the environment and check whether it satisfies the user’s request.

And sometimes there isn’t a simple programmatic check. You can use another model to evaluate what happened, but then you have to ask how reliable that evaluator is. Because whatever you use as the reward, that’s what the agent is going to learn to optimize. So getting that verification right is a really important part of making reinforcement learning work.

r001.rationale: The response recommends checking the resulting environment state against the user’s request, but does not propose comparing the tool call’s returned result with a known correct response.
